issues.description: In Experiment 2, the token-based interaction between specificity and condition is reported with z = 0.60 and p < 0.01. A z-value of 0.60 corresponds to a two-tailed p-value of approximately 0.55, making p < 0.01 impossible. Either the z-value or the p-value is incorrectly reported, and this error undermines the conclusion that the token-based specificity analysis supports the hypothesis.
issues.quote: for the token analyses - z = 0.60, p < 0.01

issues.subcategory: Conflicting values between text and table
issues.description: The go-past time congruency effect is reported with different parameter estimates and test statistics in the text versus Table 5. The text reports B = 41, t = 3.837, while Table 5 reports B = 43, t = 3.76. These should be identical since they describe the same analysis. This discrepancy calls into question which values are correct.
issues.quote: There was an effect of congruency on go-past time (B = 41, t = 3.837, p < 0.001)

issues.subcategory: Conflicting values between text and table for regressions-out
issues.description: The regressions-out congruency effect is reported with different parameter estimates and test statistics in the text versus Table 5. The text reports B = 0.3, z = 3.12, p < 0.01, while Table 5 reports B = 0.25, z = 2.65, p < 0.01. These values are substantially different for the same analysis.
issues.quote: The effect of congruency on regressions-out was significant in the expected direction, i.e. incongruent targets were more likely to elicit regressions to earlier regions of the sentence (B = 0.3, z = 3.12, p < 0.01).

issues.description: The authors state that 154 suffixes were identified in total and that 64 suffixes occurring in fewer than 20 words were excluded, leaving '95 suffixes.' However, 154 - 64 = 90, not 95. There is a discrepancy of 5 suffixes that is unaccounted for.
issues.quote: we excluded all suffixes that occur in fewer than 20 different words in the CELEX database, i.e. 64 suffixes (Baayen et al., 1993). For the remaining 95 suffixes

issues.description: Comprehension accuracy is reported as '0.86%' which literally means 0.0086 or less than 1% accuracy. This is clearly intended to be 86% (or 0.86 as a proportion). This error could mislead readers about the quality of the eye-tracking data and participant engagement.
issues.quote: Average accuracy on comprehension trials was 0.86% (ranging from 0.66% to 0.98%).

issues.description: The number of words before the target nonword differed significantly between congruent and incongruent conditions (p < 0.05). While the authors attempt a post-hoc statistical control by adding the interaction to the model, this confound should have been eliminated at the design stage. Context length differences could affect expectations and reading strategies independently of the suffix manipulation.
issues.quote: Note that the number of words pre-target was slightly different across conditions (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05).

issues.description: Six eye-tracking measures were tested (skipping, first fixation, first run dwell time, go-past time, regressions-in, regressions-out) without any correction for multiple comparisons. With six tests at α = 0.05, the family-wise error rate is substantially inflated. The authors acknowledge no predictions about which measures would be affected, making this an exploratory analysis that should be treated with appropriate correction or caution.
issues.quote: We did not have any concrete predictions as to which eye-movement measures would be affected by the diagnosticity manipulation, so we chose to monitor a variety of typically studied measures

issues.description: No pre-registration is mentioned for any of the three experiments. Given the multiple dependent variables in Experiment 3, the exploratory nature of many analyses (e.g., separate analyses for adjective- and noun-diagnostic suffixes in Experiment 1, testing whether diagnosticity/specificity interactions improve model fit), and flexibility in choosing which measures to emphasize, pre-registration would have been important for distinguishing confirmatory from exploratory analyses.
issues.quote: Data for all experiments can be found in the OSF storage for this project.

issues.description: No a priori power analyses are reported for any of the three experiments (N = 46, 29, and 47 respectively). Without power analyses, it is impossible to evaluate whether the studies were adequately powered to detect the predicted effects, particularly the graded effects of diagnosticity/specificity which are likely smaller than the main congruency effects.
issues.quote: Participants were 46 undergraduate students at Royal Holloway, University of London.

issues.subcategory: Exclusion of adverbs from lexical category analysis
issues.description: The analysis considers only three lexical categories (nouns, adjectives, verbs) but excludes adverbs. This is problematic because the most frequent suffix in the dataset, -LY (type frequency = 2717), is overwhelmingly adverbial. Its diagnosticity values for nouns, adjectives, and verbs sum to only 0.047, making it appear non-diagnostic when it is in fact highly diagnostic for adverbs. Similarly, -ALLY (type frequency = 397) shows zero diagnosticity for all three categories. This omission inflates the apparent diagnosticity/specificity of the suffix system for the included categories and provides a distorted picture of suffix-meaning relationships.
issues.quote: Our analyses consider three major lexical categories: nouns, adjectives, and verbs.

issues.description: In Experiment 1, random intercepts are included for subjects and suffixes, but not for individual nonword items. Since each suffix appears with multiple nonwords (4 per suffix), variability across items sharing the same suffix is not modeled. This could lead to underestimated standard errors and inflated Type I error rates, as item-level variance is conflated with suffix-level effects.
issues.quote: This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject) + (1|suffix), data, family = "binomial").

issues.description: Across all three experiments, only random intercepts are reported. No random slopes for the key effects (e.g., condition by subject, condition by suffix) are included or justified. Barr et al. (2013) have shown that omitting random slopes can inflate Type I error rates. The authors do not discuss why maximal or more complex random effects structures were not used.
issues.quote: We included two random intercepts, one for subjects and one for suffixes.

issues.subcategory: Overclaiming functional adaptation of spelling system
issues.description: The authors claim that English spelling 'may have become fractionated in such a way that the high degree of spelling-sound inconsistency maximises the transmission of meaningful information.' This is a strong functional/teleological claim based on correlational data. The entropy analysis shows a slope of 0.9 (spelling vs. phonology), which is a very modest difference. No causal mechanism is provided for how spelling systems could optimize for meaning transmission, and alternative explanations (e.g., historical accidents, etymological preservation) are not adequately ruled out.
issues.quote: English spelling may have become fractionated in such a way that the high degree of spelling-sound inconsistency maximises the transmission of meaningful information.

issues.description: In the diagnosticity analysis for regressions-out in Experiment 3, the effect in the incongruent condition is described as showing a 'trend towards an effect' at p = 0.13 for go-past times, and as 'marginal significance' at p = 0.08 for regressions-out. These non-significant effects are interpreted as supporting the hypothesis, which could mislead readers about the strength of the evidence for graded diagnosticity effects.
issues.quote: whereas there was a trend towards an effect in the incongruent condition (B = 36.35, t = 1.58, p = 0.13)

issues.subcategory: Inability to distinguish morphological from orthographic cues
issues.description: The authors acknowledge that they did not include non-pseudoaffixed control conditions in Experiment 1, making it impossible to determine whether participants are responding to morphological knowledge specifically or to lower-level orthographic regularities. This is a critical limitation for the theoretical interpretation, as nonmorphological ending cues (discussed in the paper's own section on orthography and morphology) could explain the results.
issues.quote: We did not include non-pseudoaffixed words because the goal of this experiment was not to adjudicate between types of cues used in lexical category judgement (e.g. orthographic vs morphological).

issues.description: All three experiments used undergraduate students from a single university (Royal Holloway, University of London). The results are generalized to 'skilled readers' and 'literate adults' broadly, but the sample is limited in age, education level, and likely socioeconomic background. No demographic details beyond native English speaker status are provided.
issues.quote: We have shown that the average reader learns and subsequently relies on morphological cues to class even without explicit instruction

issues.description: 11.7% of data points were missing in Experiment 1 due to timeouts or non-response button presses. This is a substantial data loss rate for a simple binary classification task with a 2-second response window. The authors do not analyze whether data loss was systematic (e.g., more missing for certain suffixes or conditions), which could introduce bias.
issues.quote: 11.7% of data points were missing due to timeouts or button presses that did not correspond to a response

issues.description: In Experiment 1, suffixes with diagnosticity ≥ 0.50 were selected. For a binary noun-adjective classification task, 0.50 is chance level. The suffix -AN has noun diagnosticity of 0.504 and adjective diagnosticity of 0.496, providing essentially no discriminative information. Including such suffixes conflates 'diagnostic' and 'non-diagnostic' items, and their inclusion could dilute effects or create noise.
issues.quote: These suffixes all had a high diagnosticity, i.e. greater than or equal to 0.50, and occurred in at least 20 different words.

issues.description: Diagnosticity is P(category|spelling) and specificity is P(spelling|category, sound sequence). These are related through Bayes' theorem: P(category|spelling) ∝ P(spelling|category) × P(category). The authors treat these as conceptually independent constructs but never discuss this mathematical relationship, which constrains the degree to which they can vary independently and affects interpretation of their correlation (r = 0.53).
issues.quote: Conceptually, diagnosticity and specificity are distinct theoretical constructs, since one describes the mapping from writing to meaning, while the other characterises the mapping from meaning to writing.

issues.description: Each participant heard all 66 sentences, experiencing every suffix in both congruent and incongruent contexts. Exposure to a suffix in a congruent context could prime or alter spelling behavior for the same suffix in the incongruent context (or vice versa). No counterbalancing across participants for order of congruent/incongruent presentations of the same suffix is reported.
issues.quote: Each subject saw all 66 sentences.

issues.subcategory: Missing details on spelling response variability
issues.description: In Experiment 2, the dependent variable is binary (target spelling vs. other spelling), but no information is provided about what the 'other' spellings actually were, how many unique spellings were produced, or whether spelling errors unrelated to the suffix were common. This information is needed to evaluate the validity of the binary coding scheme.
issues.quote: Suffix spellings were manually extracted from whole nonword spellings (1,914 analysable data points). The dependent variable was binary and coded whether the actual spelling was the target spelling for this suffix or not

issues.description: Participants were explicitly told to decide if nonwords 'look like' a noun or adjective and given definitions of these categories. This instruction may have encouraged explicit strategic reasoning rather than tapping implicit knowledge. The authors later claim this knowledge reflects implicit statistical learning, but the task itself is highly explicit.
issues.quote: You will be asked to decide if a letter string looks like a noun or an adjective. NOUN is a person, animal, place, thing, or idea

issues.description: The authors claim that knowledge of suffix-category relationships was 'acquired through implicit statistical learning processes' rather than explicit instruction. However, no evidence is presented to distinguish implicit from explicit learning. Participants could have learned these relationships through explicit morphological instruction in school (e.g., learning about suffixes like -NESS, -OUS). The claim requires evidence that was not collected.
issues.quote: It is unlikely that our participants were ever taught these relationships explicitly; more likely is that this knowledge was acquired through implicit statistical learning processes

issues.description: For the eye-tracking analyses, the authors state they included trial order as a main effect and random intercepts for subjects and suffixes, but relegate full model results to supplementary materials. Key details such as whether random slopes were tested, model comparison criteria, and handling of the continuous dependent variables' distributional assumptions (e.g., log-transformation of reading times) are not reported.
issues.quote: All models included trial order as a main effect, and random intercepts for subjects and for suffixes. However, in the interest of space we report only those effects pertaining to our main variable of interest

issues.description: The authors report a slope of 0.9 for the regression of Hspelling on Hphonology, with a slope significantly different from 1 (F(1) = 7.44, p < 0.01). However, the F-test has only 1 numerator degree of freedom reported without the denominator degrees of freedom, making it impossible to evaluate. More importantly, a slope of 0.9 could arise from many factors (e.g., regression to the mean, differential measurement error) and does not necessarily mean spelling is more informative than phonology about category.
issues.quote: We found that the regression line has a slope of 0.9 (SE = 0.04, t = 25.32, p < 0.0001), and that this slope is significantly different from 1 (F (1) = 7.44, p < 0.01).

issues.subcategory: Pseudosuffix inclusion may bias diagnosticity estimates
issues.description: The computational analysis intentionally includes pseudoaffixed words (e.g., VANISH for -ISH, CORNER for -ER) in diagnosticity calculations. While justified by evidence that readers parse these morphologically, this inclusion systematically reduces diagnosticity estimates because pseudoaffixed words may not share the category of genuinely affixed words. This creates a potential mismatch between the corpus-derived measures and the genuine morphological knowledge being tested behaviorally.
issues.quote: we also needed to capture words in which the suffix spellings do not function as genuine morphemes (e.g. the –ER in 'corner').

issues.description: Across all experiments, token-based measures of diagnosticity and specificity consistently provided poorer fits than type-based measures. The authors note this but do not provide a satisfactory explanation. Given that token frequency is typically a stronger predictor than type frequency in psycholinguistic research, this unexpected pattern raises questions about what the type-based measures are actually capturing (e.g., whether they are confounded with other suffix properties).
issues.quote: Token-based analyses showed a weaker effect of diagnosticity, which we will return to in the General Discussion.

issues.description: No standardized effect sizes (e.g., Cohen's d, odds ratios, R²) are reported for any of the three experiments. Only unstandardized regression coefficients and test statistics are provided, making it difficult to evaluate the practical significance of the effects or to compare across studies.
issues.quote: Results showed a main effect of suffix condition such that noun-diagnostic suffixes elicited more "noun" responses (B = -1.57, z = -4.224, p < 0.0001)

issues.description: In Experiment 3, 40 filler nonwords with verb-diagnostic suffixes were included but not analyzed because 'the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category.' This means one-third of the experimental trials are discarded, reducing power, and the exclusion of verbs limits the generalizability of claims about suffix-category relationships in reading.
issues.quote: These filler nonwords were not analysed, because the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category (i.e. diagnosticity is less than 0.5).

issues.subcategory: Claims about English writing system evolution
issues.description: The authors speculate that the proliferation of spellings in English 'may actually be functional' and that 'irregularity in the English spelling-sound mapping may permit regularity in the spelling-meaning mapping.' This functional-evolutionary claim about orthographic design is not testable with the present synchronic data and extends well beyond what the behavioral experiments demonstrate.
issues.quote: This fractionation could not occur in a spelling-sound transparent writing system.
